Des agents de code via Tailscale
Tailscale 経由のコーディングエージェント
通过 Tailscale 使用编程智能体
透過 Tailscale 使用程式設計代理

description.p: Tailscode drives the coding agents running on your other machines. The agent stays where your code is; this is the window onto it, over your own tailnet, with nothing in between.
It speaks to Claude Code (through claude-bridge) and to opencode, and it is a native GTK4 application rather than a web view.
What it does:

ul.li: Watch an answer arrive at reading speed, with tool calls, diffs and images inline
Approve or refuse what the agent wants to run, from the conversation
Split the window into panes — several chats, a terminal, the file tree, a browser
See what a conversation has cost and what the month has cost, priced per turn
Read the repository the agent is working in: branch, diff, and what it has touched
Keep every server up to date from inside the app, and be told honestly when it cannot

description.p: Clicking through chats is quick and always lands: the sidebar redraws only the row that changed instead of rebuilding the whole list, and never while the mouse is down. Expanding a tool call while the answer is still being written always registers, and a finished conversation holds still — tool marks and workflow circles stop the moment the turn ends.

Answer statistics split the wait the way it actually splits: time to first token is its own figure and tokens per second is measured over the generation that followed, with the model's average on this device behind it. The model chooser explains itself on a right click, a failed tool call closed by hand stays closed, and a workflow card settles the moment every agent has finished.

The answer pushes the page up as it is written. Sending still lifts the prompt to the top of the window, and the transcript now holds still until the written words actually reach the bottom — it used to start scrolling early, chasing text that was laid out but not yet shown. A picture sent with a message rises with the words instead of hiding a line above the top edge, a message sent is on screen the instant it is sent even while the conversation is still loading, and a short conversation no longer reads as already full when a prompt rises.

The model picker starts with the machine: every server is a tab, and under it the providers are a filter — one chip per subscription or key, so you read what Ollama Cloud, OpenCode Go or OpenRouter will run as one list and a pick goes through that door. A model wears its own name (gpt-oss-120b, never a bare GPT), and a heading's chevron always points the way the list is folded.

A queued message belongs to its conversation: it survives a restart, goes the moment its turn yields whichever chat is on screen, and never lands in another chat — switching chats used to carry it along. Oh My Pi conversations name themselves and every Oh My Pi session has a real per-turn ledger; a sent message is drawn exactly like a sent message from the keystroke, and only a failure changes its ink.

Oh My Pi joins Claude Code and opencode as a first-class agent everywhere, Quick Ask aims with real server and model menus, the model directory has stars, Usage has an Ollama Cloud meter, a turn's clock counts from its own prompt, and the jump-to-bottom button is simply the way back.

Ask for a video and watch it being made: an agent renders it on one of your machines while the app follows the work, and the finished film is kept right there. The renderer has its own studio now — one walk sets it up, the model list is a picker you aim into, settings open as a menu, and the chip wears the machine that answered.

The composer grows a third lane beside chat and ask, and the send wears the lane it is sending down. When a provider refuses a request mid-turn, the card says what happened and offers the same words again without the pictures.

A machine that stops answering stops its clocks. A conversation's age counted on whether or not the server holding it was still reachable, so a turn that ended hours ago kept ageing on a laptop that had been asleep since. The column now freezes at the moment that machine was last heard from, and a live card over a server that has gone quiet says so instead of claiming the turn is still running.

A running turn's clock actually runs. The time beside a live conversation only moved when the list was refetched, so it sat still and then jumped. It now counts second by second, without asking any server anything, and holds still the moment there is nothing to count.

New models turn up on their own. A server that had been running for days was still offering the model list it resolved the day it started, so a model your plan gained this week was out of reach until somebody restarted it by hand. The opencode setup command now leaves a check on that machine which notices and restarts it — never in the middle of a turn — and the picker takes the newer list without waiting for a relaunch.

A server can be started over from here. Where a server is explained there is now one press for it, which is the only way back, from the device in your hand, to anything a long-running process reads once at startup: its models, its config, its plugins. It says what it would stop before it does it.

A turn whose machine went says so. A server that stops mid-answer leaves a conversation that reads as a question nobody answered — the prompt is there, no answer follows, and nothing says one was ever coming. It now says what happened, what the work had got through, and offers to pick it back up. And a machine holding a build it has never started is marked in the list rather than hidden behind the trust that keeps it current, because that is work no update will do for you.

Keeping your machines current is the app's job now. A server that already has a newer build sitting on it is one press away from running it, and a machine you trust can take its updates by itself — always waiting until nothing is running on it, so a restart never pulls the floor out from under a turn.

Clearing what you missed now clears it. Notices you had already dealt with came back on their own moments later, because emptying the list left the notifications themselves standing. And the Home screen redraws only the cards that actually changed, so a busy fleet no longer makes it stutter.

A slash command now runs on the model the chat is wearing. Running /command said nothing about which model should answer it, so the server used its own default — and the chat then took that model's name, which is why a conversation could start as one model and quietly become another. Commands, compactions and goals all carry the model and effort named above the box now.

A chat that is connected says so. A conversation nobody was talking in used to sit under "connecting" indefinitely, even while its own transcript, its cost and its branch were all on screen — the app was only ever guessing at the connection from how recently something had been said. It now reads the socket itself, and a connection that really is taking a while counts up so you can see it.

A turn the machine was pulled out from under is no longer a question that looks ignored. When a server is updated, killed or loses power mid-answer, the chat now says what happened, how far the work actually got — which files were written, what commands ran, how far the answer had come — and offers to pick it back up or let it go.
Typing a folder for a new chat now completes against the real disk on the machine that will host it, the way a shell does: press tab, get the rest of the name.

Chats on a home-directory workspace stream live again. A message sent from Linux or the phone to an opencode session rooted outside the server's project list used to run on the machine — you could watch the GPU work — while the app sat still. The client now finds that session's workspace and follows the turn as it is written.

A turn that comes back with nothing now says so. A model can finish a turn having produced no answer, no tool call and no error at all — most often when the question carried a picture its provider will not take — and until now the whole turn was invisible: the spinner stopped and the transcript sat exactly as it was, as if the question had been ignored. The chat now states what happened, quotes the server's own word for the ending, and offers to ask again — without the picture, when that is what it choked on.

Quick Ask hands its question over properly. Asked at the wrong moment — while another screen was still animating — it could open the conversation and never send the words. The question now travels with the conversation it was asked in, and the sheet slides away onto a chat that is already holding it, in one movement rather than two.
An answer that stopped mid-sentence now finishes.

A streamed reply is played out at reading speed rather than painted in the lumps the network delivers, and a turn that ended at exactly the wrong moment could leave the last paragraph holding half a sentence — with the rest of it already on the phone. The transcript now measures what actually reached the screen instead of trusting the count, and a paragraph it could not hand over whole is tried again until it lands.

The transcript has stopped moving under you. A row keeps its name while its contents change, so a card no longer blinks out and back when the agent revises its plan or a picture finishes loading, and one row changing no longer rebuilds everything under it. Text that arrives while the app is catching up now lands in the paragraph it was being written into rather than above the tools that interrupted it. A code block types out instead of freezing and dumping, and nothing that has reached the screen ever leaves it again.

Type does more of the talking. Your prompt and the answer are set as a question and the paragraph under it — the prompt the heavier voice, the answer the lighter one with the air — a tool's name outweighs its arguments, and every size in the app comes from one ramp rather than a guess per screen. Anything that changes while you watch it is set in figures of equal width, so a settled number no longer reads as movement.

Quick Ask is no longer a text box. It is the chat's own composer: pictures, files, a paste that becomes the file it already is, and an empty state that offers the first half of a question instead of a placeholder — narrowed to what the model you picked can actually read, with the last few questions asked on that machine one tap from reopening.
Also: tapping a turn-done notification opens the chat instead of closing the app, and a quota banner no longer mistakes a long reply for a spent limit.

A chat running at full power now looks it, wherever you open it. Ultracode started on another machine arrives on your phone wearing its aura, and a turn summoned with the word lights up on every device watching that conversation.

Missed knows what it is pointing at. A notice raised before the server had named the chat now carries the words that started it instead of “New chat”, and the list takes the real name the moment it lands. It also drops what has stopped being true — a chat you deleted, or one that is working again — and picks up turns that finished while the app was closed. Everything since 1.3, in one update.
TROPHIES. Every turn you have ever run is read into a trophy case — achievements, leaderboards and the marks you are closest to earning, with Game Center behind it and nothing to sign up for.

YOUR MONEY, AND YOUR LIMITS. A chat now carries what the whole conversation has spent, and touching it opens the account: per turn, where the money went, which model spent it. The month has its own surface — every machine's ledger merged into one, with your quotas leading on the window that decides when the next send unlocks. And a used-up limit speaks only where it applies: the model picker shows what is spent and when it comes back.

YOUR SERVERS KEEP THEMSELVES CURRENT. The app watches every machine in the picture and wears one quiet mark when an update is waiting — no alert, nothing to dismiss — and one press installs it and follows the server through its own restart.

READING A CONVERSATION. Code is coloured by what it is, in whatever theme you are wearing, and a diff shows its additions and removals. Tables render as real columns. An address written in prose is one you can tap. A picture the agent hands you opens as a gallery you can zoom, save and share. A compaction reads as a seam with its summary a tap away, and the agent's plan is one live board instead of twenty snapshots.

FINDING YOUR WORK. Pin the chats you keep coming back to; a busy row names the tool it is out on, and reads as three facts at three weights. A project opens as its own board. Where a change is landing — the branch, and what has been touched — rides the chrome and opens read-only. Drafts survive leaving a chat.

GETTING STARTED. The app goes and finds your machines instead of asking you to type an address, a chat that cannot start says why and offers the one thing that fixes it, and the install command on the setup screen is the installer.
Plus ultracode, new themes including Suomi, and long-pressing the Home screen icon takes you straight where you were going.
See what a conversation has cost: tap the figure in a chat and the whole account opens — per turn, where the money went, which model spent it.

Pin the chats you keep coming back to, and a busy row now names the tool it is out on. A run of agent steps folds into one line instead of a stack of cards, drafts survive leaving a chat, and long-pressing the icon on the Home screen takes you straight where you were going.

Code reads as code. Every fenced block is now coloured by its language — keywords, names, strings, comments — in whatever theme you are wearing, and a diff shows its additions and removals. Long lines scroll instead of folding.
